claim: Habit formation is a behavioral adaptation that automates routine actions.
source: Habit formation is a behavioral adaptation that automates routine actions.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about habit formation presented in the abstract.

claim: Habitual behavior correlates with broad reconfigurations of dorsolateral striatal (DLS) circuit properties that increase gain and shift pathway timing.
source: Habitual behavior correlates with broad reconfigurations of dorsolateral striatal (DLS) circuit properties that increase gain and shift pathway timing.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to prior work (O'Hare et al., 2016) as indicated in the introduction.

claim: Fast-spiking interneurons (FSIs) modulate all habit-predictive properties of striatal output.
source: Here we find that a single class of interneuron, fast-spiking interneurons (FSIs), modulates all of these habit-predictive properties.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 1 and 2 showing FSI modulation of SPN firing properties.

claim: FSIs are more excitable in habitual mice compared to goal-directed mice.
source: Consistent with a role in habits, FSIs are more excitable in habitual mice compared to goal-directed
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 3 showing increased FSI firing in habitual mice.

claim: Acute chemogenetic inhibition of FSIs in DLS prevents the expression of habitual lever pressing.
source: acute chemogenetic inhibition of FSIs in DLS prevents the expression of habitual lever pressing
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 4 showing that chemogenetic inhibition of FSIs blocks habit expression.

claim: FSIs inhibit most SPNs but paradoxically promote the activity of a subset displaying high fractions of gamma-frequency spiking.
source: In vivo recordings further reveal a previously unappreciated selective modulation of SPNs based on their firing patterns; FSIs inhibit most SPNs but paradoxically promote the activity of a subset displaying high fractions of gamma-frequency spiking.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo recording data presented in Figure 5.

claim: The dorsolateral region of the striatum has been heavily implicated in the formation and expression of habits through lesion and inactivation studies.
source: The dorsolateral region of the striatum has been heavily implicated in the formation and expression of habits through lesion and inactivation studies (Yin et al., 2004; Yin et al., 2006)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Properties of the dorsolateral striatum (DLS) input-output transformation of afferent activity to striatal projection neuron firing predict the extent of habitual behavior in individual animals.
source: More recently, properties of the dorsolateral striatum (DLS) input-output transformation of afferent activity to striatal projection neuron firing were found to predict the extent of habitual behavior in individual animals (O'Hare et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: DLS output arises from striatal projection neurons (SPNs), which comprise ~95% of striatal neurons.
source: DLS output arises from striatal projection neurons (SPNs), which comprise ~95% of striatal neurons
evidence: This is a statement of established anatomical knowledge about striatal composition.

claim: SPNs project to either the direct (dSPNs) or indirect (iSPNs) basal ganglia pathways.
source: striatal projection neurons (SPNs), which comprise ~95% of striatal neurons and project to either the direct (dSPNs) or indirect (iSPNs) basal ganglia pathways
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about basal ganglia circuitry.

claim: The properties of evoked SPN firing ex vivo linearly predict behavior across the goal-directed to habitual spectrum in an operant lever pressing task.
source: The properties of evoked SPN firing ex vivo linearly predict behavior across the goal-directed to habitual spectrum in an operant lever pressing task (O'Hare et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Habitual responding correlates with larger evoked responses in both the direct and indirect pathways.
source: Specifically, habitual responding correlates with larger evoked responses in both the direct and indirect pathways
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (O'Hare et al., 2016).

claim: Habitual responding correlates with a shorter latency to fire of dSPNs relative to iSPNs.
source: habitual responding correlates with larger evoked responses in both the direct and indirect pathways as well as a shorter latency to fire of dSPNs relative to iSPNs
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (O'Hare et al., 2016).

claim: IEM-1460 decreased the amplitude of evoked calcium transients in both dSPNs and iSPNs.
source: IEM-1460 decreased the amplitude of evoked calcium transients in both dSPNs (t(86) = 3.42, p=0.001, n = 87) and iSPNs (t(51) = 2.11, p=0.040, n = 52).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: IEM-1460 changed the relative latency to fire between direct and indirect pathway SPNs by increasing the pre-existing bias whereby iSPNs respond to cortical excitation more quickly than dSPNs.
source: IEM-1460 also changed the relative latency to fire between direct and indirect pathway SPNs by increasing the pre-existing bias in relative pathway timing whereby iSPNs tend to respond to cortical excitation more quickly than dSPNs (Figure 1F)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: IEM-1460 selectively reduced calcium transient amplitudes of high-firing SPNs but not low-firing SPNs.
source: According to this pre-IEM-1460 categorization, low-firing SPNs were unaffected whereas calcium transient amplitudes of high-firing SPNs were significantly reduced by IEM-1460 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Basal calcium transient amplitudes linearly predicted the inhibitory effect of IEM-1460 in both SPN subtypes.
source: Consistent with a selective inhibition of multi-action potential responses, basal calcium transient amplitudes linearly predicted the inhibitory effect of IEM-1460 in both SPN subtypes (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: IEM-1460 did not affect spike probability in either SPN subtype.
source: Moreover, IEM-1460 did not affect spike probability in either SPN subtype (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: IEM-1460 predominantly weakens excitatory synaptic inputs onto FSIs in striatum.
source: To manipulate FSI activity, the calcium-permeable AMPA receptor (CP-AMPAR) antagonist IEM-1460, which predominantly weakens excitatory synaptic inputs onto FSIs in striatum (Gittis et al., 2011b), was used.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Striatal FSIs express AMPARs lacking the GluA2 subunit, rendering them permeable to calcium.
source: Striatal FSIs express AMPARs lacking the GluA2 subunit, rendering them permeable to calcium (Hollmann et al., 1991)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: SPNs do not typically express CP-AMPARs.
source: whereas SPNs do not typically express CP-AMPARs
evidence: This is established knowledge about SPN receptor expression.

claim: IEM-1460 does not affect excitatory synaptic currents in SPNs but strongly decreases excitatory transmission onto FSIs.
source: Consistent with this difference in AMPAR subunit expression, IEM-1460 does not affect excitatory synaptic currents in SPNs but strongly decreases excitatory transmission onto FSIs (Gittis et al., 2011b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: IEM-1460 reduced synaptically-evoked AP firing in FSIs in the acute parasagittal DLS preparation.
source: Cell-attached FSI recordings before and after exposure to IEM-1460 (50 μM) confirmed the drug's efficacy to reduce synaptically-evoked AP firing in our acute parasagittal DLS preparation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Optical inhibition of PV+ interneurons reliably decreased evoked SPN firing.
source: We found that optical inhibition of PV+ interneurons reliably decreased evoked SPN firing (Figure 2C, left and middle panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Single-action potential events and failures in SPNs were unaffected when FSIs were silenced.
source: Analysis of SPN responses by trial (paired consecutive laser OFF/ON sweeps), rather than by cell, indicated that single-action potential events and failures were unaffected when FSIs were silenced (Figure 2C, right panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: FSIs promote multi-action potential SPN responses to cortical excitation in the brain slice.
source: this optogenetic result indicates that FSIs promote multi-action potential SPN responses to cortical excitation in the brain slice
evidence: This claim is inferred from the optogenetic experiments showing that silencing FSIs reduces multi-AP responses.

claim: No difference was detected in sEPSC frequency or amplitude between goal-directed and habitual FSIs.
source: No difference was detected in sEPSC frequency or amplitude between goal-directed and habitual FSIs (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Paired-pulse ratios of evoked EPSCs measured at a 50 ms inter-stimulus interval were similar between goal-directed and habitual FSI groups.
source: Additionally, paired-pulse ratios of evoked EPSCs measured at a 50 ms inter-stimulus interval were similar between groups (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: FSIs from habitual mice displayed higher firing rates compared to FSIs from goal-directed mice.
source: FSIs from habitual mice displayed higher firing rates compared to FSIs from goal-directed mice (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The duration over which firing could be sustained markedly differed between goal-directed and habitual FSIs.
source: However, the duration over which firing could be sustained markedly differed between the two behavioral groups (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The majority of FSIs from goal-directed mice were unable to maintain high-frequency firing for the entire duration of the 500 ms current injection.
source: The majority of FSIs from goal-directed mice were unable to maintain high-frequency firing for the entire duration of the 500 ms current injection (<250 ms of firing in 10/15 cells)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data analysis.

claim: Nearly all FSIs from habitual mice maintained high-frequency firing for the duration of current injection.
source: whereas nearly all FSIs from habitual mice maintained such activity (>450 ms firing in 7/9 cells)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data analysis.

claim: FSIs of habitual mice fired more readily than those from mice with goal-directed behavior in response to electrical stimulation of excitatory afferents.
source: We found that FSIs of habitual mice fired more readily than those from mice with goal-directed behavior (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of PV+ interneurons did not affect operant behavior in general, as evidenced by indistinguishable lever press rates between groups in the non-devalued condition.
source: Chemogenetic inhibition of PV+ interneurons did not affect operant behavior in general, as evidenced by indistinguishable lever press rates between groups in the non-devalued (grain pellets) condition (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Habit expression was suppressed in PV-hM4D mice relative to PV-eYFP controls.
source: In contrast, a comparison of sensitivity to outcome devaluation between groups revealed that habit expression was suppressed in PV-hM4D mice relative to PV-eYFP controls (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: RI-trained PV-eYFP control mice were insensitive to outcome devaluation (habitual).
source: Mean NDLPr for RI-trained PV-eYFP control mice measured at 0.46 ± 0.27, indicating that control mice were insensitive to outcome devaluation, i.e. habitual.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data analysis.

claim: PV-hM4D mice displayed sensitivity to outcome devaluation (goal-directed responding) despite receiving the same RI training schedule.
source: By contrast, PV-hM4D mice, which received the same RI training schedule and showed comparable rates of lever pressing (Figure 4C), displayed a mean NDLPr of −0.60 ± 0.30. A negative NLDPr indicates sensitivity to outcome devaluation, i.e. goal-directed responding.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data analysis.

claim: CNO significantly decreased FSI firing rates compared to vehicle-injected controls.
source: As expected for the inhibitory hM4D receptor, CNO significantly decreased FSI firing rates compared to vehicle-injected controls (CNO: 59.61 ± 8.08% baseline; vehicle: 86.89 ± 11.66% baseline) (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Suppressing FSI activity caused an overall increase in SPN firing (disinhibitory effect) relative to vehicle.
source: we further found that suppressing FSI activity caused an overall increase in SPN firing (i.e. disinhibitory effect) relative to vehicle (CNO: 472.00 ± 149.12%; vehicle: 188.02 ± 45.94%; Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The baseline fraction of ISIs falling within the gamma-frequency band linearly predicted how firing rates in individual SPNs changed when FSI activity was suppressed.
source: We found that the baseline (pre-CNO) fraction of ISIs falling within the highest rate frequency band, gamma-frequency (30–100 Hz), linearly predicted how firing rates in individual SPNs changed when FSI activity was suppressed (Figure 5G, left; see Figure 5—figure supplement 1 for example units).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: SPNs with higher fractions of gamma-frequency ISIs at baseline are more likely to decrease firing rate when FSIs are inhibited with CNO.
source: That is, the higher the fraction of gamma-frequency spikes an SPN fired, the more likely it was to fire less when FSIs were chemogenetically inhibited.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the correlation analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: No relationship between gamma ISI fraction and firing rate modulation was observed in response to vehicle.
source: No such relationship was observed in response to vehicle (Figure 5G, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The proportion of gamma-frequency ISIs was unrelated to mean firing rate in baseline single unit SPN recordings.
source: However, we found that the proportion of gamma-frequency ISIs was unrelated to mean firing rate in baseline single unit SPN recordings before either CNO or vehicle administration (pre-CNO: p=0.25, n = 23; pre-vehicle: p=0.28, n = 20).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: SPNs fire significantly more gamma-frequency spikes than expected by Poisson processes matched to firing rate.
source: Additionally, we found that SPNs fire significantly more gamma-frequency spikes than expected by Poisson processes matched to firing rate (pre-CNO: t(44) = 5.76, p=7.67×10−7, n = 23 SPNs and rate-matched simulations; pre-vehicle: t(38) = 8.24, p=5.59×10−10, n = 20 SPNs and rate-matched simulations).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison to simulated data.

claim: Baseline excess probability of gamma-frequency ISIs specifically predicts rate modulation after CNO but not vehicle.
source: the excess probability of gamma-frequency ISIs (observed – expected) specifically predicts rate modulation after CNO (r(22) = −0.52, p=0.011, n = 23) but not vehicle (r(19) = 0.045, p=0.85, n = 20)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Parvalbumin-positive, fast-spiking interneurons (FSIs) provide the strongest source of local modulation in the striatum.
source: Among the various interneuron types resident to the striatum (Tepper et al., 2010), parvalbumin-positive, fast-spiking interneurons (FSIs) provide the strongest source of local modulation
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: FSIs exert strong, feedforward inhibition of SPNs via perisomatic GABAergic contacts onto virtually all SPNs.
source: exerting strong, feedforward inhibition of SPNs via perisomatic GABAergic contacts onto virtually all SPNs (Gittis et al., 2010; Koós and Tepper, 1999; Koos et al., 2004; Mallet, 2005; Taverna et al., 2007; Straub et al., 2016; Szydlowski et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: FSIs are expressed in the dorsal striatum on a mediolateral gradient with the most residing in DLS.
source: Notably, FSIs are expressed in the dorsal striatum on a mediolateral gradient with the most residing in DLS (Gerfen, 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: FSIs preferentially innervate dSPNs relative to iSPNs.
source: FSIs also preferentially innervate dSPNs relative to iSPNs (Gittis et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Striatal FSI plasticity has been demonstrated through experimenter-induced activity and genetic manipulations.
source: Striatal FSI plasticity has been demonstrated through experimenter-induced activity and genetic manipulations (Mathur et al., 2013; Winters et al., 2012; Orduz et al., 2013; Gittis et al., 2011a)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Acute suppression of FSI activity in DLS causes habit-trained subjects to behave as though they were goal-directed.
source: These findings show that acute suppression of FSI activity in DLS causes habit-trained subjects to behave as though they were goal-directed.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the behavioral data showing that FSI inhibition blocks habit expression.

claim: Fewer striatal FSIs have been observed in human brains from individuals with Tourette's syndrome.
source: For example, fewer striatal FSIs, as determined by parvalbumin-immunopositivity, have been observed in human brains from individuals with Tourette's syndrome (Kalanithi et al., 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Fewer striatal FSIs have been observed in mouse brains in a model of OCD-like behavior.
source: fewer striatal FSIs, as determined by parvalbumin-immunopositivity, have been observed in human brains from individuals with Tourette's syndrome (Kalanithi et al., 2005) and mouse brains in a model of OCD-like behavior (Burguière et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: OCD is highly comorbid in Tourette's syndrome.
source: OCD is highly comorbid in Tourette's syndrome (Sheppard et al., 1999)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Disrupted habit learning has been implicated in pathological compulsivity in a variety of settings.
source: disrupted habit learning has been implicated in pathological compulsivity in a variety of settings (Graybiel, 2008; Everitt and Robbins, 2005; Gerdeman et al., 2003)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Lower parvalbumin levels are associated with a hyperexcitable FSI phenotype.
source: Lower parvalbumin levels are associated with a hyperexcitable FSI phenotype (Orduz et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Glutamatergic corticostriatal synapses express dopamine-dependent forms of long-lasting synaptic potentiation and depression.
source: Glutamatergic corticostriatal synapses express dopamine-dependent forms of long-lasting synaptic potentiation and depression (Shen et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Synaptic plasticity at corticostriatal synapses accompanies changes in behavior, including the formation of habits.
source: Although such plasticity accompanies changes in behavior, including the formation of habits (Shan et al., 2015; Nazzaro et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Interneurons are often anatomically suited to tune SPN activity in a broad manner through extensive axonal arbors.
source: Because interneurons are often anatomically suited to tune SPN activity in a similarly broad manner through extensive axonal arbors (Kawaguchi et al., 1995; Tepper et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Habit-predictive striatal output properties are relatively uniformly distributed when elicited by strong bulk stimulation of cortical afferents.
source: Based on the previous observation that habit-predictive striatal output properties are relatively uniformly distributed when elicited by strong bulk stimulation of cortical afferents (O'Hare et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Spatially-clustered SPN activity encodes information relevant to locomotor behavior.
source: Indeed, recent evidence suggests that spatially-clustered SPN activity encodes information relevant to locomotor behavior (Barbera et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: IEM-1460 has an inhibitory effect on FSI and SPN spike probability as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.
source: Effects of IEM-1460 on FSI and SPN spike probability are shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.
evidence: This claim references data shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: Drug wash-in significantly inhibited FSI firing (t(5) = 4.08, p=0.0096, n = 6 cells).
source: Drug wash-in significantly inhibited FSI firing (t(5) = 4.08, p=0.0096, n = 6 cells).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Drug wash-in did not affect spike probability for dSPNs (p=0.055, n = 87) or iSPNs (p=0.11, n = 52).
source: Drug wash-in did not affect spike probability for dSPNs (p=0.055, n = 87) or iSPNs (p=0.11, n = 52).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: IEM-1460 consistently reduced SPN responses to singlets (r(7) = 0.94, p=0.00060, n = 8 cells).
source: IEM-1460 consistently reduced SPN responses to singlets (r(7) = 0.94, p=0.00060, n = 8 cells)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Vehicle had no effect on SPN responses (mean effect = 0.28 ± 0.66; p=0.89 for correlational analysis, n = 8 cells).
source: whereas vehicle had no such effect (mean effect = 0.28 ± 0.66; p=0.89 for correlational analysis, n = 8 cells)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: 532 nm light strongly inhibits evoked FSI firing (t(5) = 15.54, p=0.000020, n = 6 cells).
source: 532 nm light strongly inhibits evoked FSI firing (t(5) = 15.54, p=0.000020, n = 6 cells).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Inhibition of striatal FSIs caused SPNs to fire fewer action potentials (t(12) = 3.33, p=0.0060, n = 13 cells).
source: Inhibition of striatal FSIs caused SPNs to fire fewer action potentials (t(12) = 3.33, p=0.0060, n = 13 cells).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: PV-Arch effectively blocked evoked FSI firing.
source: In this configuration, PV-Arch effectively blocked evoked FSI firing (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 532 nm light drove outward currents in FSIs but not SPNs.
source: Control experiments showed that, as predicted, 532 nm light drove outward currents in FSIs but not SPNs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Arch expressed in PV+ cells (PV-Arch) abolished high-frequency firing of FSIs in response to somatic current injection.
source: Additionally, Arch expressed in PV+ cells (PV-Arch) abolished high-frequency firing of FSIs in response to somatic current injection (Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: PV-Arch had no effect on SPN firing in the same recording configuration.
source: and had no effect on SPN firing in the same recording configuration (Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Goal-directed and habitual mice used for group-wise comparisons of electrophysiological properties did not differ in total number of lever presses (p=0.72, n = 7 and 5 mice).
source: Goal-directed (orange) and habitual (purple) mice used for group-wise comparisons of electrophysiological properties did not differ in total number of lever presses (p=0.72, n = 7 and 5 mice)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Goal-directed and habitual mice did not differ in number of rewards delivered (p=0.72, n = 7 and 5 mice).
source: or number of rewards delivered (p=0.72, n = 7 and 5 mice, Mann-Whitney U test) over the course of training
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: No differences were found in passive membrane properties of FSIs between goal-directed and habitual mice (p=0.13, 0.081, 0.67, 0.58, n = 15 and 9 cells).
source: No differences were found for any membrane property (p=0.13, 0.081, 0.67, 0.58, n = 15 and 9 cells).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E-H.

claim: No difference was detected in action potential waveform properties between goal-directed and habitual FSIs (p=0.60, 0.71, 0.53 n = 13 and 8 cells).
source: No difference was detected for any waveform property (p=0.60, 0.71, 0.53 n = 13 and 8 cells).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Mice from both PV-hM4D and PV-eYFP groups learned the task similarly (p=0.70, n = 10 and 11 mice).
source: Learning curves for hM4D and reporter construct-injected cohorts show that groups did not learn the task differently (p=0.70, n = 10 and 11 mice).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: PV-hM4D mice showed less habit expression relative to PV-eYFP controls (t(19) = 2.66, p=0.016, n = 10 and 11 mice).
source: PV-hM4D mice showed less habit expression relative to PV-eYFP controls (t(19) = 2.66, p=0.016, n = 10 and 11 mice).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Mice expressing hM4D and eYFP in FSIs of the DLS did not differ in response rates in the non-devalued condition (p=0.53, n = 10 and 11 mice).
source: Mice expressing hM4D and eYFP in FSIs of the DLS did not differ in response rates (p=0.53, n = 10 and 11 mice)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: CNO- and vehicle-treated subjects did not respond differently to i.p. injections (p=0.16 for interaction of time and treatment, n = 6 and 7 mice).
source: group-wise quantification of distance travelled shows that CNO- and vehicle-treated subjects did not respond differently to i.p. injections (p=0.16 for interaction of time and treatment, n = 6 and 7 mice)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Subjects non-specifically decreased locomotor activity following the i.p. injection procedure (F(11,1) = 49.01, p=2.27×10−5, n = 6 and 7 mice).
source: Subjects non-specifically decreased locomotor activity following the i.p. injection procedure (F(11,1) = 49.01, p=2.27×10−5, n = 6 and 7 mice).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: FSI waveforms display a shorter spike width relative to those of SPNs (t(64) = 30.67, p=5.53×10−40, n = 23 FSIs and 43 SPNs).
source: FSI waveforms display a shorter spike width relative to those of SPNs (t(64) = 30.67, p=5.53×10−40, n = 23 FSIs and 43 SPNs).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: FSIs display higher firing rates than SPNs (t(64) = 4.32, p=0.000056, n = 23 FSIs and 43 SPNs).
source: FSIs display higher firing rates than SPNs (t(64) = 4.32, p=0.000056, n = 23 FSIs and 43 SPNs).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: CNO injection decreased FSI firing rate relative to vehicle (interaction between drug and time: F(5,105) = 2.51, p=0.034, n = 13 and 10 FSIs).
source: CNO injection decreased FSI firing rate relative to vehicle (interaction between drug and time: F(5,105) = 2.51, p=0.034, n = 13 and 10 FSIs).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: CNO injection increased SPN firing rate relative to vehicle (interaction between drug and time: F(5,205) = 2.63, p=0.025, n = 23 and 20 SPNs).
source: CNO injection increased SPN firing rate relative to vehicle (interaction between drug and time: F(5,205) = 2.63, p=0.025, n = 23 and 20 SPNs).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: SPNs with higher fractions of gamma-frequency ISIs at baseline are more likely to decrease firing rate when FSIs are inhibited with CNO (r(22) = −0.59, p=0.0032, n = 23 cells).
source: SPNs with higher fractions of gamma-frequency ISIs at baseline are more likely to decrease firing rate when FSIs are inhibited with CNO (r(22) = −0.59, p=0.0032, n = 23 cells)
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Vehicle caused no change in firing rate that could be predicted by baseline fraction of gamma ISIs (p=0.92, n = 20 cells).
source: whereas vehicle caused no change in firing rate that could be predicted by baseline fraction of gamma ISIs (p=0.92, n = 20 cells)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Habitual FSIs fired at an overall higher rate relative to goal-directed FSIs (F(1, 22) = 5.84, p=0.024, n = 15 and 9 cells).
source: Habitual FSIs fired at an overall higher rate relative to goal-directed FSIs (F(1, 22) = 5.84, p=0.024, n = 15 and 9 cells).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Goal-directed FSIs are less-able to sustain firing than habitual FSIs (U = 34.5, p=0.049, n = 15 and 9 cells).
source: Goal-directed FSIs are less-able to sustain firing than habitual FSIs (U = 34.5, p=0.049, n = 15 and 9 cells).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Goal-directed response durations were bimodally distributed (p=0.020, Hartigans' dip test).
source: Goal-directed response durations were bimodally distributed (p=0.020, Hartigans' dip test).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: When accounting for response duration, no difference in firing rates is observed between goal-directed and habitual FSIs (p=0.25, n = 15 and 9 cells).
source: When accounting for response duration, no difference in firing rates is observed (p=0.25, n = 15 and 9 cells).
